newsitem.title: USA: New EU gene label "not a big deal" - US ag analysts.
newsitem.headline: New EU gene label "not a big deal" - US ag analysts.

text.p: U.S. agribusiness analysts Thursday said new labelling requirements by the European Union for genetically-modified farm products were "not a big deal" and had been widely expected.

Analysts said the rules require labels for all new gene-altered seeds, a move companies will want to make because it helps them differentiate their products. Gene-altered seed is identified in the United States.
The requirement does not apply to Monsanto Co's Roundup Ready soybean seed or any other gene-altered seed that had already won EU approval.
"It's not a big deal. But it does show Europe is pretty serious about providing information," said Michael Green of GRi Intl., an agribusiness consultant firm in Kansas City.
The European Commission Wednesday approved rules that require labels specify a product "may contain or may consist of genetically modified organisms" (GMOs) from July 31.

Analysts noted the new EU gene label requirements were issued by the commission's environment arm and that the agriculture secretariat, led by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, had a gene labelling proposal in the pipeline.
Fischler has been seeking segregation of GMO products throughout the food chain and compulsory labelling.

Timothy Galvin, associate administrator at the U.S. Agriculture Department's Foreign Agricultural Service predicted Fischler's proposal would be pushed back until late July or perhaps end of summer. He said EU ministers will meet July 2 on novel foods regulations, which also affect biotech products.
"It's (Fischler's proposal) viewed as more Draconian than the other measures so they want to walk before they can run on this thing so they can work through these issues," he said.
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman told a grain group in London Thursday the U.S. would not tolerate segregating gene-altered crops.
U.S. officials say such a move could disrupt trans-Atlantic trade and that the U.S. would seek a World Trade Organization dispute panel if the EU adopts such a requirement.
